newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - Mexico seen far from debt rating upgrade.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mexico seen far from debt rating upgrade.

text.p: When Mexico repaid early $5 billion of international emergency loans last month, rumours began circulating in financial markets that the country's debt rating would be increased, perhaps as early as this spring.
But while Mexico's economy may be back on the road towards good growth, analysts and debt raters are ruling out any quick increase in its debt standing.
They say there are still just too many barriers in the way.

"In spite of Mexico's economy clearly going in the right direction, we don't believe there will be an increase in Mexico's sovereign debt rating until GDP is able to grow at sustained rates of at least 5.0 percent without causing a balance of payments crisis, which unfortunately has not been the case in the last three decades," said a report by the brokerage house Interacciones.
SET BACK BY PESO AND STOCK MARKET CRASH
Before the peso crash in 1994, Mexico flirted with the coveted investment grade rating, a level held only by Chile and Colombia among Latin American countries.

Mexico was basking in the glow of a successful start to the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), investors were happy to pour money into its markets, and its image abroad was for the most part still positive.
Many government officials then expected the country would soon receive the important investment grade rating.
That rating would signal a much lower probability of default, and allow a broader base of investors to buy Mexico's debt issues. It could also narrow the spread on debt issues that Mexico floats.
The ratings agencies held back, however.

"There was a popular consensus that Mexico should be upgraded, if you recall, because of the stability of the (former president Carlos) Salinas regime and the policies that were irreversable, and then it was going to be a member of NAFTA," said Moody's Investors Service analyst Nina Ramondelli.
"But we were very afraid of what could occur and which indeed did occur," she said.
A rebel uprising, two high-level political assassinations, and too much short-term debt financing a huge current account deficit helped spark a peso crisis in December 1994 and a stock market crash.
Interest rates and inflation rose and the economy tumbled into recession the following year.
THE RATINGS
The ratings agencies are once again taking a cool approach to Mexico.
When asked if Mexico is in line for a ratings increase, Ramondelli said :"We are very happy with the rating at this time."
Moody's has a Ba2 rating on Mexico. That is two below an investment grade rating and Ramondelli says for the rating to jump to an investment grade would require, "truly extenuating circumstances".
Mexico does not appear to fit in that category.
Standard & Poor's first gave a BB+ to Mexico, but then placed it on a credit watch after the devaluation of the peso. The rating was later downgraded to BB with a negative outlook.
In September, S & P's lifted Mexico's outlook to stable from negative on the United Mexican States' long-term foreign currency obligations.
"There is a stable outlook and we feel that this is appropriate where it is," said S & P's sovereign debt analyst Lacey W. Gallagher.
She noted that ratings are based on long-term factors, and when asked if Mexico might soon receive an investment grade rating she said :"The short answer is no."
Another rating agency agreed.
"We need to see some more improvement in the qualitative factors," said Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Co vice-president Andres O'Byrne.
"We have Mexico two notches away from an investment rating, as have S & P and Moody's. I don't think that in the next year, Mexico will be able to achieve an investment grade rating."

O'Bryne added that while Mexico's early prepayment of what it owed to the U.S. Treasury from its part in the bailout of Mexico after the peso crash was a welcome sign, in itself it would not be enough to spur a ratings increase.
THE CONSTRAINTS
One important barrier to a credit upgrade is the deeply troubled Mexican banking system, with many of the weaker banks kept afloat only with expensive government support.
That weak financial system is seen as hobbling growth.
Weak domestic savings, the need to improve the competitiveness and the efficiency of the economy, and the fluctuations of the political reform process are also negative factors, analysts added.
High interest rates, a fall in real wages and high unemployment are seen keeping political pressure on the government's strict monetary and fiscal policies.
Mexico's foreign debt load is also a negative factor.
"It has a huge foreign debt, and large debt servicing requirements, while Chile and Colombia have relatively smaller debts," Ramondelli said.
Also high on the list are concerns over political uncertainty.
The rocky process of political liberalisation, which aims to give Mexico a more open political system, could affect confidence and economic activity, the rating agencies said.
